tasks.description: Create a tuple `coords = (10, 20, 30)`. Print the second element.
tasks.hint:
Tuples use the same index syntax as lists: `tuple[index]`
Zero-based: first element is `[0]`, second is `[1]`, third is `[2]`.
`coords[1]` → `20`
tasks.walkthrough: Tuples are indexed from 0 like lists, so position 1 is the second item, 20.

tasks.description: Unpack the tuple (1, 2, 3) into three variables a, b, c and print their sum.
tasks.hint:
Tuple unpacking assigns each element to a variable in one line.
`a, b, c = (1, 2, 3)` — the number of variables must match the tuple length.
Then `print(a + b + c)` → `6`
tasks.solution:
a, b, c = (1, 2, 3)
print(a + b + c)
tasks.walkthrough:
Three names on the left, three items on the right, so each name gets one item.
Then it's simple addition.

tasks.description: Try to change the first element of (1, 2, 3) to 99. Notice what error appears — tuples are immutable.
tasks.hint:
Tuples are IMMUTABLE — once created, their contents cannot be changed.
Trying `t[0] = 99` raises a `TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment`
This is intentional — use a list if you need to modify elements.
tasks.walkthrough:
Assigning to `t[0]` raises a TypeError because tuples can't be modified.
Wrapping it in `try`/`except` lets the program show the message instead of crashing. You'll learn try/except properly tomorrow.
Without the try, you'd see the red error box in this app, which is also fine for this task.

tasks.description: Create a set from the list [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4]. Print the set. Notice duplicates are removed.
tasks.hint:
`set()` converts any iterable to a set, automatically removing duplicates.
`set([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4])` → `{1, 2, 3, 4}`
Sets are unordered — the printed order may vary, but the values are correct.
tasks.walkthrough:
`set()` keeps one copy of each value and throws the rest away.
For small integers Python happens to print them in ascending order.

tasks.description: Find the common elements (intersection) of sets {1, 2, 3, 4} and {2, 4, 6}. Print sorted.
tasks.hint:
Intersection = elements that appear in BOTH sets.
Use `&` operator: `{1,2,3,4} & {2,4,6}` → `{2, 4}`
Or `.intersection()`: `s1.intersection(s2)`
`sorted(result)` gives a consistent order for testing.
tasks.walkthrough:
`&` is intersection: the values that appear in both sets, which are 2 and 4.
`sorted()` turns the result into a list in order, so the output is predictable.

tasks.description: Find the unique elements from both sets {1, 2, 3} and {2, 3, 4, 5} combined (union). Print sorted.
tasks.hint:
Union = ALL elements from BOTH sets (no duplicates).
Use `|` operator: `{1,2,3} | {2,3,4,5}` → `{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}`
Or `.union()`: `s1.union(s2)`
`sorted(result)` for consistent ordering.
tasks.walkthrough:
`|` is union: everything in either set, with duplicates removed.
Sorting gives [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].

tasks.description: Use a set to count how many UNIQUE characters are in the string 'mississippi'. Print the count.
tasks.hint:
`set(string)` treats each character as an element, removing duplicates.
`set('mississippi')` → `{'m', 'i', 's', 'p'}` — only 4 unique chars.
`len(set('mississippi'))` → `4`
tasks.walkthrough:
A string is a sequence of characters, so `set()` collects the distinct ones: m, i, s, p.
`len()` counts them, giving 4.

lesson.intro:
Two more containers. A tuple is a list you can't change, useful for things that
belong together like coordinates. A set is a bag of unique items with no order,
useful for removing duplicates and asking "have I seen this before?".

sections.heading: Tuples
sections.body:
Round brackets instead of square. Indexing works the same as with lists.
What you can't do is change an item after the tuple is made. That
immutability is the point: it says "this is fixed".

sections.heading: Unpacking
sections.body:
You can pull the items of a tuple into separate variables in one line.
The number of names on the left has to match the number of items.
This is what's happening when a function returns two values.
sections.code:
a, b, c = (1, 2, 3)
print(a + b + c)

sections.heading: Sets remove duplicates
sections.body:
`set()` turns any collection into a set, dropping repeats. Curly braces also
make a set (with no colons; colons would make a dictionary). Sets have no
order, so don't rely on the position of anything.

sections.heading: Combining sets
sections.body:
`&` gives the items in both sets. `|` gives the items in either. `-` gives
the items in the first but not the second. Wrap the result in `sorted()`
when you want a predictable order.

watch_out: `t[0] = 99` on a tuple gives a TypeError. That's by design. Use a list if it needs to change.
A tuple with one item needs a trailing comma: `(5,)`. Plain `(5)` is just the number 5.
`{}` makes an empty dictionary, not an empty set. For an empty set write `set()`.
Sets don't support indexing. `my_set[0]` is an error.
